title: Shadow-TTL with tenant-aware LRU arbitration and epochal correctness proofs
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: With continuous batching and aggressive GPU memory optimization we see increased eviction churn for small prefix-scoped KV entries under mixed tenant workloads. This causes higher cold-start latency and occasional correctness alerts when inflight batches expect cached KV that was evicted prematurely.

Proposal: Implement a shadow-TTL regulator layered on top of an LRU arbitration policy that is tenant-aware and uses epochal snapshots to produce eviction proofs. Key ideas: 1) Maintain a lightweight shadow-TTL that decays more slowly for prefixes observed to be repeatedly referenced across batched requests; 2) Use tenant-scoped LRU buckets to bias eviction away from prefixes with cross-request reuse while preserving overall fairness; 3) Introduce an epoch fence and per-epoch eviction proof ledger so that any in-flight request can verify a prefix was not evicted during its execution window, enabling safe demotion to CPU memory or eviction only after proof epochs complete.

Why this approach: continuous batching extends effective lifetime of KV hits across multiple requests since batches share sequence prefixes; a static TTL or pure LRU misses this temporal locality signal. Shadow-TTL captures observed reuse without changing global TTL semantics, enabling safer eviction decisions while limiting memory growth. Epochal proofs give an auditable correctness contract for in-flight operations and allow us to avoid heavy-weight locking on the hot path.

Design details: 
- Data structures: per-prefix metadata: {last_seen_epoch, shadow_ttl_score, tenant_id, last_batch_counter} stored in a compact 64-bit header (bitfields) to keep GPU memory footprint small.
- Shadow-TTL update rule: on a hit, increment score = min(score + alpha, max_score); periodically decay score per-epoch by multiplying with beta. Effective TTL = base_ttl * (1 + score_factor * score).
- Tenant-aware LRU: maintain lightweight LRU rings per-tenant (on GPU) with a global admission policy that enforces a per-tenant soft quota to avoid noisy neighbors. Eviction candidate selection: prefer lowest effective TTL across allowed tenant quota slack, fallback to global LRU when slack exhausted.
- Epochal eviction proofs: eviction operations are emitted with a monotonically increasing epoch id. Inflight requests record the epoch at start and check the ledger on completion; evictions in the same or later epoch are guaranteed not to invalidate the request's cached prefix. Ledger entries are compact (epoch -> bitmap of slots) and rotated.
- Demotion policy: entries with low shadow score and small memory footprint are opportunistically demoted to CPU backing store rather than fully evicted, saving GPU cycles while maintaining correctness for rare reuses.

Tradeoffs and risks:
- Extra metadata increases per-entry bytes; mitigated by packing header and using 8-byte per-entry target.
- Shadow-TTL tuning (alpha/beta) needs workload-driven calibration; plan to auto-tune based on observed hit-rate improvements and memory pressure.
- Ledger maintenance adds some control-plane cost; designed to be epochal and amortized to avoid hot-path latency impact.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Functionality: eviction proofs validate for 100% of in-flight requests during synthetic stress tests.
- Correctness: zero cache-related assertion failures in stress-run 48-hour fuzz run.
- Performance: under mixed-tenants replay trace, GPU resident KV memory reduced by >= 12% (vs baseline) without dropping overall token-level cache hit-rate by more than 2%.
- Latency: p95 generation latency change < 3% under standard batching traces.
- Safety: rollout behind feature flag with canary (5% traffic) and automatic rollback if errors > 0.5% or cache hit rate degradation > 5% in canary window.

Implementation plan (high-level):
1) Metadata header and compact ledger proto (spike branch).
2) Shadow-TTL computation and per-hit update path (microbenchmark).
3) Tenant LRU ring implementation with soft quotas.
4) Epochal ledger integration and correctness checks in the request lifecycle.
5) Demotion path to CPU backing store and metrics.
6) End-to-end simulation harness + fuzz tests + perf traces.
7) Canary rollout and monitoring runbook.

Docs & artifacts: design doc: https://drive.google.com/drive/fake/redwood/shadow-ttl-design (internal) PR draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5879 (WIP) Benchmark traces: gs://redwood-ci/traces/2026-02-shadow-ttl/

Notes: This ticket focuses on correctness-first design while aiming for measurable GPU memory wins. Shadow-TTL is intentionally conservative at first (low alpha) to avoid over-retention and will be tuned from telemetry during canary.
